slides.label: Route
slides.notes: Open the appendix as a convention-management lecture. The mathematics is not introducing a brand new object so much as separating several inner-product habits that appear in the literature. Tell students that every later proof is also a software lesson about choosing a grade rule and keeping it auditable.

slides.label: Product Family
slides.notes: Use the switchboard as the high-level map. Left contraction is deliberately asymmetric, right contraction is its opposite-side partner, the dot product chooses the lower-grade side, and the Hestenes variant adds scalar exceptions. The practical question is which convention leaves the fewest hidden branches in an algorithm.

slides.label: Left Contraction
slides.notes: Spend time on the visual interpretation before the formulas. A left contraction asks what remains in the larger blade after the left operand has been matched metrically. The vector-plane example is small enough to compute aloud and strong enough to show why zero can carry geometric information.

slides.label: Right And Dot
slides.notes: Present the right contraction as the same selection idea viewed from the other side, then show why the dot product feels symmetric in many examples. The branch line is useful for compact notation, but it also means the operation changes behavior when input grades cross.

slides.label: Grade Grid
slides.notes: Read the grid as an implementation contract rather than as a table to memorize. Each colored lane tells a programmer which grade may survive. The important point is that left and right contractions preserve containment tests, while dot-style products move that decision into a grade comparison.

slides.label: Agreement Cases
slides.notes: This is the reconciliation slide. When the lower non-scalar grade is written first, the common conventions agree, so formulas transfer between books with little drama. The exceptions are exactly the places where a library should expose its convention instead of pretending all inner products are interchangeable.

slides.label: Recursive Vector Rule
slides.notes: Work the alternating sum as a deletion rule. The vector tests each generator by the metric, removes that generator from the blade, and keeps the signed leftover span. The notebook check gives a concrete result that students can recompute from two dot products and one sign change.

slides.label: Adjoint Test
slides.notes: Frame the implicit definition as an adjoint relationship with the outer product. Instead of treating contraction as a bag of special cases, the scalar product test says that wedging on one side and contracting on the other are paired operations. Nondegenerate metrics make this pairing unique.

slides.label: Second Duality
slides.notes: Use the containment picture to keep the duality statement from becoming pure symbol pushing. The condition that A sits inside C is not cosmetic; it prevents extra terms from appearing. The proof ladder shows how a vector identity grows into a blade identity by induction.

slides.label: Projection Norm
slides.notes: Connect the appendix proof back to the geometric operation students already use. Contracting into a non-null blade and multiplying by the inverse blade returns the projected component, while the norm relation says the contraction length measures the size of that component scaled by the blade.

slides.label: Implementation Cautions
slides.notes: This slide should feel like a code review checklist. Grade branches, scalar exceptions, degenerate blades, and convention aliases are not philosophical details; they decide whether a geometric algebra package returns zero, a lower-grade blade, or an exception. The notebook artifacts make those decisions testable.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by turning the appendix into a reusable habit. First name the geometric question, then choose the product convention, then check the grade and any inverse blade, and finally compare against a small basis-blade ledger. That workflow keeps literature notation and executable code aligned.
